(CNN) -- He was not able to fulfill his childhood dream of being a pilot, but Ghanaian scientist Dr. Ave Kludze has arguably gone one better: developing and flying spacecrafts for NASA. The moon, Mars and beyond: All are in the sights of Dr. Ave Kludze. The 43-year-old didn't enter orbit when controlling a NASA rocket to launch the Calipso environmental satellite in 2006, instead piloting it from the control center on the ground. Nevertheless from growing up in Ghana to being an astronautical engineer and strategist for NASA, he has had a similarly stratospheric rise to the top. Growing up in Accra, Kludze was fascinated by science and how things worked. "I was a very curious kid and I always questioned lots of things, and most of my friends I grew up with, they knew that. And my parents, they were a little bit concerned because sometimes I would take apart a lot of things they would not want me to touch," he told CNN. When he realized he could not become a pilot because of his eyesight he channeled his energies into studying engineering, moving to the U.S. to complete a course in electrical engineering at Rutgers University. On graduating Kludze initially planned to return to Ghana to develop solar technologies, but then NASA came calling in 1995. "I never did dream of working for NASA. I admired what they did, but it never did cross my mind. I did not see how a kid like me could work for NASA," he said. He commanded his first spacecraft from NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center and has gone on to develop an extra-vehicular infra-red camera as well as other projects for the space agency. While he didn't return to Ghana as he originally planned, he still believes that his work -- and NASA's -- has had some benefits to his native country and more down-to-earth lives. "Well, NASA has done a lot for Africans. Maybe Africans they no know that. They have cell phones, glasses, anti-scratch and all those things. We have portable water system that NASA has developed for Africa. They're using it," he said. "And one thing people often forget, NASA doesn't only develop space technology, we also develop aeronautical technology. So when the planes they fly and other flying objects, NASA's technology has been involved in that." Kludze is also keen to pass on the message that for young Africans, the sky is the limit in terms of what they do with their lives. "I've learned that being given the freedom to think and think openly helps bring in new ideas. So in community, like in an African communities, I think younger generations and both the old and the young should freely share ideas and break those old barriers. "So I believe that with some determination and some hard work most of the younger generation can get whatever they want to. They can even go into space, they can do anything."

The moon, Mars and beyond are all within Dr. Kludze’s sights. Although the 43-year-old did not enter orbit when he controlled a NASA rocket launching the CALIPSO environmental satellite in 2006—instead piloting it from a ground-based control center—his journey from Ghana to becoming an astronautical engineer and strategist for NASA has been similarly stratospheric.

Growing up in Accra, Kludze was fascinated by science and by understanding how things worked.

“I was a very curious kid, and I always questioned lots of things. Most of the friends I grew up with knew that. And my parents were a little bit concerned because sometimes I would take apart a lot of things they would not want me to touch,” he told CNN.

When he realized he could not become a pilot because of his eyesight, he redirected his ambitions toward engineering, moving to the United States to study electrical engineering at Rutgers University.

After graduating, Kludze initially planned to return to Ghana to develop solar technologies. But in 1995, NASA came calling.

“I never did dream of working for NASA. I admired what they did, but it never did cross my mind. I did not see how a kid like me could work for NASA,” he said.

He commanded his first spacecraft from NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center and went on to develop an extra-vehicular infrared camera, along with other projects for the space agency.

Although he did not return to Ghana as originally planned, Kludze still believes that his work—and NASA’s—has benefited his native country and improved more down-to-earth aspects of daily life.

“Well, NASA has done a lot for Africans. Maybe Africans they no know that. They have cell phones, glasses, anti-scratch and all those things. We have portable water system that NASA has developed for Africa. They’re using it,” he said.

“And one thing people often forget: NASA doesn’t only develop space technology; we also develop aeronautical technology. So when the planes fly and other flying objects, NASA’s technology has been involved in that.”

Kludze is also eager to share the message that, for young Africans, the sky is the limit when it comes to what they can achieve in life.

“I’ve learned that being given the freedom to think, and to think openly, helps bring in new ideas. So in a community, like in African communities, I think younger generations—and both the old and the young—should freely share ideas and break those old barriers.

“So I believe that with some determination and some hard work, most of the younger generation can get whatever they want to. They can even go into space; they can do anything.”

**By CNN-style Feature Staff**

When Dr. Kofi Mensah was a child growing up in Ghana, he would lie outside at night and stare at the sky, trying to make sense of the stars that seemed to stretch endlessly above his family’s home.

“I was the kind of child who took apart radios, flashlights, anything I could get my hands on,” Mensah said. “My mother used to say, ‘Kofi, one day you will either fix the world or break everything in the house.’ But I was just curious. I wanted to know how things worked.”

That curiosity would eventually carry him thousands of miles from West Africa to the United States, where he studied electrical engineering and later joined NASA, contributing to satellite systems and space-based technologies used to monitor Earth’s climate, weather, agriculture and natural resources.

For Mensah, now a senior engineer at NASA, the journey from a small community in Ghana to one of the world’s leading space agencies was never only about reaching the stars. It was also about looking back at Earth — especially Africa.

“Space technology is not distant from everyday life,” he said. “It helps farmers know when to plant. It helps communities prepare for floods. It helps governments track drought, fires and changing coastlines. These are not abstract scientific ideas — they affect real people.”

Mensah moved to the United States as a young man to pursue electrical engineering, a field he saw as the bridge between his childhood fascination with machines and his desire to solve practical problems.

“When I arrived in America, everything felt bigger — the campuses, the labs, the expectations,” he said. “But I carried with me the same questions I had as a child: How does this work? How can it help people? And how can I bring some of this knowledge back to Africa?”

At NASA, Mensah has worked on systems that support Earth-observing missions, including satellite instruments that collect data on vegetation, rainfall, temperature and atmospheric conditions. Such data is used by scientists, humanitarian organizations and governments around the world.

In Africa, where climate change is intensifying droughts, floods and food insecurity in many regions, satellite data can be especially valuable. Earth-observation tools help monitor crop health, forecast extreme weather and track water resources across vast areas where ground-based monitoring may be limited.

“NASA’s work benefits Africa every day, even when people don’t realize it,” Mensah said. “The same satellites that help scientists study global climate patterns can help a farmer in Kenya, a disaster response team in Mozambique or water managers in the Sahel.”

Mensah says he is particularly passionate about expanding access to scientific data and encouraging young Africans to see themselves as future engineers, physicists, climate scientists and space researchers.

“The most powerful thing about space exploration is perspective,” he said. “From space, you don’t see borders the way we draw them on maps. You see one planet, connected. And that reminds me why this work matters.”

As NASA continues to expand its partnerships and open more data to researchers around the world, Mensah hopes the next generation of African scientists will not see space as something far away, but as a tool for solving urgent challenges at home.

“When I look at Africa, I don’t just see problems to solve,” he said. “I see innovation, resilience and possibility. Space technology can be part of that future — and African scientists should help lead it.”
